READING

**Setting up the numbers**

The base to beat is £143,000 a year from all 640 colonies on your own sites, with zero haulage and zero spray risk. Per colony that is £223 (rounding for readability). The problem tells us borage alone returned £71 a colony, so heather accounts for roughly £152 a colony.

Under TREVANNOCK the 400 Vantwyn colonies miss the borage window but can reach heather in August. The income picture per Vantwyn season is:

| Item | £ |
|---|---|
| Pollination fee (400 × £168) | +67,200 |
| Borage foregone (400 × £71) | −28,400 |
| Haulage and labour | −6,900 |
| Spray replacements (9 % × 400 = 36 colonies × £210) | −7,560 |
| **Net annual gain over the ORMSCLEUCH baseline** | **+24,340** |

Over the three contracted seasons that is **£73,020** of additional operating cash compared with running all 640 on your own ground.

**The asset value gap**

Ravensgate will pay £96,000 now. Once the permit lapses on 1 January 2030 (the morning after the last Vantwyn season ends) the lorry is a farm vehicle worth roughly £20,000. The kit therefore costs you **£76,000** in terminal value if you choose TREVANNOCK instead of selling now.

Running the totals in nominal terms over the three seasons:

| | ORMSCLEUCH | TREVANNOCK |
|---|---|---|
| Honey revenues (own sites, all colonies or remaining 240) | £429,000 | £160,875 |
| Heather from Vantwyn colonies (post-loss) | — | £182,928 |
| Pollination fees | — | £201,600 |
| Less: borage foregone | — | −£85,200 |
| Less: haulage | — | −£20,700 |
| Less: spray replacements | — | −£22,680 |
| Asset realisation | +£96,000 | +£20,000 |
| **Three-year total** | **£525,000** | **£522,000** |

The margin is roughly **£3,000 in ORMSCLEUCH's favour** on a like-for-like nominal basis—barely perceptible. But three factors then push the gap further in the same direction.

**Time value.** The £96,000 lands before the first Vantwyn hive is loaded. The £20,000 arrives after the permit has gone. Even at a modest discount rate the present-value gap between those two receipts is meaningfully larger than the headline £76,000 versus £73,020 suggests.

**Risk asymmetry.** The 9 % figure is a single observation from Whinnerdale in one season on a spray programme Vantwyn will not vary. If losses run to 12 % the replacement bill rises to £10,080 a season (£30,240 over three years) and TREVANNOCK slides clearly negative. If losses hit 15 % the bill is £12,600 a season. There is no upside scenario that improves on 9 %; Vantwyn's rigid programme makes it a one-tail risk.

**The "staying in the market" argument is hollow.** Coldharbour and Nyefield are asking for 2028 rates. Under TREVANNOCK, 400 of your 640 colonies are committed to Vantwyn for all three seasons, leaving 240 colonies to service your own sites. There is nothing spare to offer either vale grower in 2028. By the time the Vantwyn deal finishes, the lorry has lost its vale low-emission-zone permit anyway, so any subsequent vale work would require a new compliant vehicle—another capital call on top of the £76,000 already forgone. TREVANNOCK does not buy re-entry to the vale; it merely delays the moment at which you acknowledge you have left it, while running up costs along the way.

**The queen rearing shed** is absent from the Ravensgate offer and stays on your books under either course. It remains useful for raising replacement queens in your own operation regardless of which path you take; it does not tip the scales.

**Summary verdict**

ORMSCLEUCH and TREVANNOCK are nominally within £3,000 of each other over three years, but every additional consideration—time value of money, spray-loss risk, the impossibility of serving Coldharbour and Nyefield during the Vantwyn commitment, and the lorry's imminent permit expiry—favours selling the kit now and concentrating entirely on heather and borage. The sunk £187,000 from 2024 is irrelevant to this choice; it is gone under both courses. What is not yet gone is £96,000 of recoverable asset value, and TREVANNOCK's best-case three-season gain does not quite cover it.

---

READING
The three contracted Vantwyn seasons generate a nominal operating surplus of £73,020 over the ORMSCLEUCH baseline, but the difference between the Ravensgate offer (£96,000, received immediately) and the post-permit residual value of the lorry (£20,000, received after 2029) is £76,000; time value widens that gap further, spray-loss risk is one-tailed and falls entirely on TREVANNOCK, and the "remaining in the vale market" argument fails because all 400 portable colonies are locked to Vantwyn throughout the period while the lorry's permit expires the moment the contract ends.

CALL
ORMSCLEUCH

GROUNDS
The £96,000 asset realisation received immediately exceeds the entire three-season operating advantage of the Vantwyn contract before spray-loss risk or time value is applied, and the strategic argument for keeping the migratory kit running collapses once it is clear that no colonies are free for the vale growers during the contract years and the lorry loses its vale permit the day the last Vantwyn season ends.
